kurz: Why the price of a share is a fixed fact while its value can only be estimated as a range, and what a discount to the estimated value has to achieve.

bloecke.md:
The price of a share is a fact. It is in the order book, applies to everyone and can be read to the exact cent. The value of the same company, by contrast, depends on assumptions about a future that nobody knows. All the methods in this module build on this difference, and it also sets their limit. The calculations are exact, but their inputs are always uncertain.

The [[Intrinsic value|intrinsic value]] of a company is the [[Present value|present value]] of what its owners can take out of it over its remaining life. This definition comes from John Burr Williams (1938). It has been refined since, but not replaced. Three of its properties make it hard to apply. First, it requires payments, not profits. Second, it extends to the end of the company's life. Third, it needs an interest rate that compensates for time and risk. This interest rate cannot be measured; it rests on judgement.

bloecke.formel:
Value = sum over t of Z(t) / (1 + r)^t

Special case of perpetual growth:  Value = Z(1) / (r − g)
bloecke.erklaerung: The second line condenses the sum in the first line for the case where the payment grows permanently at the same rate. It shows that every valuation depends on the difference between two estimated percentages in the denominator.
variablen: payment to the owners in year t, not reported profit
discount rate: the return required for time and risk
permanent growth of the payments, necessarily smaller than r

bloecke.md:
The first property, the focus on payments instead of profits, is the one most often overlooked. Profit arises when revenue is realised, regardless of when money flows. Depreciation and provisions reduce profit without any money flowing out. Capital expenditure and growing [[Working capital|working capital]], on the other hand, consume money without reducing profit. A company can therefore report profits for years and still become insolvent.

For this, Buffett coined the term [[Owner earnings|owner earnings]] in 1986 in the appendix to the Berkshire annual report. It means reported earnings plus depreciation and other non-cash charges, less the average annual maintenance capital expenditure. In Buffett's own words, the last item must be a guess, because the balance sheet shows it nowhere. The range of the estimate therefore begins with the quantity being discounted, and not only with the discount rate.

bloecke.titel: Model company with three estimated inputs
bloecke.md:
A manufacturer with no financial debt is expected to generate €100 million of [[Free cash flow|free cash flow]] next year and has 50 million shares outstanding, which is €2.00 per share. Because there is no debt to service, the free cash flow belongs entirely to the shareholders. The discount rate used is 8.5%. This is the average [[Weighted average cost of capital (WACC)|WACC]] that KPMG determined in its 2025 cost of capital study (Kapitalkostenstudie) for around 300 mainly German companies. Without financial debt, WACC and cost of equity are the same. The cost of equity of 9.7% from the same study is an average for indebted companies and is therefore higher. Permanent growth is assumed to be 1.5%, which roughly corresponds to compensation for inflation without real volume growth.

2.00 / (0.085 − 0.015) = €28.57 per share.

This figure appears in the presentation. What is not mentioned there is that two of the three inputs are subtracted from each other in the denominator and neither of them is observable.

bloecke.titel: Value per share for twenty-five combinations of r and g
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation using Z(1)/(r − g) with Z(1) = €2.00 per share. All the assumptions are defensible, yet the most favourable and the strictest corners differ by a factor of 1.8.

bloecke.md:
The values range from €22.22 to €40.00. Half a percentage point more growth is a defensible assumption and not a sign of carelessness, and the same goes for half a point more on the discount rate. The strong effect has an arithmetical reason. The denominator contains a difference of about seven percentage points, and a shift of half a point changes this difference by around 7% of its size.

Along the diagonal, the value stays the same. If growth is raised by 0.5 points and the discount rate also by 0.5 points, the result is exactly the starting value. An optimistic and a cautious assumption can thus cancel each other out. The result then no longer reveals which assumptions went into the calculation.

bloecke.titel: A range instead of a single figure
bloecke.md: A valuation that ends with a single number is not more precise, only less well documented. The result of a valuation is an interval together with the assumptions from which it was derived. Decimal places in the result come from the arithmetic and not from precise inputs.

bloecke.titel: Shares of present value by period
bloecke.unter: Shares of present value in the model case r = 8.5%, g = 1.5%; more than half of the value arises beyond the period for which serious statements can be made.

bloecke.md:
For the next three years, well-founded statements can be made using the annual report, order backlog and knowledge of the industry. For year 24 this is not possible. Empirically, corporate growth is neither easy to predict nor stable over long periods, and forecasts more than three to five years ahead contain hardly any information. Nevertheless, more than half of the value comes from the period beyond reliable forecasts. This is not a flaw in the model that a better spreadsheet could fix; it lies in the subject of the valuation itself.

This uncertainty cannot be removed by analysis, but it can be allowed for in a businesslike way by paying less than your estimate. Graham made this discount the central concept of investing and gave the final chapter of *The Intelligent Investor* the title [[Margin of safety (Sicherheitsmarge)|Margin of Safety]]. The discount serves to offset your own estimation errors and is not intended as additional return.

bloecke.titel: Discounts to the estimated value of €28.57
kopf: Price gain up to the estimated value
Price still works at r − g of

bloecke.md: The last column translates the discount into assumptions. A purchase price of €20.00 still works even if the discount rate is three percentage points higher or growth three points lower than assumed. This is the practical purpose of the margin of safety, because it expresses caution as a number and not as a feeling. The third column also shows why the margin of safety does not act symmetrically. After a discount of 30%, the price has to rise by 43% to reach the estimated value; after a discount of 50%, it has to rise by 100%.

A discount does not replace an understanding of the business. At Wirecard, trustee account balances of €1.9 billion did not exist; that was around a quarter of the balance sheet total. If an estimate rests on assets that do not exist, even the value after a 30% discount has no basis.

A discount also says nothing about timing. A valuation contains no statement about whether and when a share price will move towards an estimate. Treating the discount as a deadline would mean confusing it with a forecast.

Nor does the discount help against systematic errors. If the assumptions are changed until the estimated value is above the share price, the margin of safety has been used up before it is deducted.

The legislator regularly has to answer the question of value. Where a price exists, it adopts that price. For listed securities, Section 11(1) BewG (Valuation Act) requires the lowest price quoted on the valuation date to be used. In this case, value is by law equal to price.

If there is no price, an estimate is made. For shares in unlisted corporations, Section 11(2) BewG requires the fair market value (gemeiner Wert). It is derived primarily from sales between unrelated third parties within the last year, otherwise from earnings prospects or another customary method, and may not be lower than the asset-based value (Substanzwert). The simplified capitalised earnings method (vereinfachtes Ertragswertverfahren) in Sections 199 to 203 BewG multiplies the sustainably achievable annual earnings by a statutory capitalisation factor of 13.75 (Section 203(1) BewG). This corresponds to an assumed rate of return of around 7.3%. The factor has applied since 2016 regardless of the prevailing market interest rate, so the discount rate for inheritance and gift tax is fixed.

For compensation payments (Abfindung) under Section 305 AktG (Stock Corporation Act) and squeeze-outs under Section 327b AktG, a court has to set an amount in appraisal proceedings (Spruchverfahren). It relies on expert opinions under the IDW S1 valuation standard and makes an estimate under Section 287 ZPO (Code of Civil Procedure). According to the DAT/Altana decision of the Federal Constitutional Court (BVerfG) of 27 April 1999, the stock market price may not be undercut in this process. Since the Stollwerck decision of the Federal Court of Justice (BGH) of 19 July 2010, the volume-weighted three-month average before the announcement of the measure has served as the reference. In these proceedings, price and value are therefore both used: value is estimated and price sets the lower limit.

A valuation is therefore not a share price forecast. It is a decision aid with three possible outcomes. The price is either clearly below the range, clearly above it or within it. The third case is the most common, and in it the right thing is to do nothing. A method that leads to action in nine out of ten cases is calculated too narrowly.

The width of the range is also information. It is narrow for a business with stable, recurring payments. It is wide for cyclical profits, high debt or a business model that is only supposed to make money years from now. The position of the price and the width of the range belong in the same decision.

bloecke.titel: Two criteria for a purchase decision
bloecke.unter: The horizontal axis shows the price relative to your own range, the vertical axis the reliability of that range; only one quadrant justifies a decision to buy.

felder.text: Stable payments, narrow range, price below it. Only here does a valuation justify action. Even here, the assumption should be recorded in writing.
The value can be estimated well, the price is above it, so no purchase. For an existing position, alternatives and tax count; being right is not a criterion.
If the range is too wide, a price below it says nothing. Typical of cyclical profits and firms without reliable payments.
Neither price nor estimate supports a purchase. This is where the most expensive positions arise, because a story replaces the calculation.

bloecke.md:
- Before calculating, note the three inputs, that is expected payment, discount rate and permanent growth, and justify each in one sentence.
- Always calculate three cases instead of just one. Only the unfavourable case is of any use later.
- Record the date, share price and range. Without the share price at the time, it is no longer possible to establish later whether the estimate or the patience was wrong.
- After twelve months, check the assumptions and not the share price. The question is whether the assumed payment materialised and, if not, whether that was due to the business or to the estimate.

Balance sheet equity is based on values from the past. Under the HGB (Commercial Code), acquisition and production costs form the upper limit of value. Self-created brands, mastheads, publishing rights and customer lists may not be capitalised at all under Section 248(2) HGB, and IAS 38 prohibits the same items. If a buyer pays for them in a takeover, they appear on the balance sheet for the first time, even though they came into being earlier.

That is why companies with brands, software and research in particular report little equity, even though their cash flows are high and stable. Capital-intensive industrial companies, by contrast, show a lot of book value and little profit. The asset-based value that Section 11(2) BewG sets as the lower limit for tax purposes is therefore only a lower limit and not a yardstick for value.

mitnehmen: The value of a company is the present value of the payments that can be taken out of it; profits and book value are not what determines it.
Because the denominator contains two estimated percentages, defensible assumptions lead to values that differ by a factor of 1.8.
More than half of the value relates to the period after ten years, for which there are no reliable forecasts.
The margin of safety offsets your own estimation errors; a 30% discount can absorb an error of around three percentage points in the denominator.
If the share price lies within the range, the valuation yields no decision.

begriffe.text: Present value of all payments that can be taken out of a company over its remaining life. Intrinsic value is an estimate with a range and not an observable market price.

Discount below the estimated intrinsic value at which you buy (Margin of Safety, Graham). It is meant to offset estimation errors. In the model Z/(r − g) with r − g = 7%, a 30% discount can absorb an error of around three percentage points in the denominator.

Tax valuation standard under Section 9 BewG, specified in more detail for shares in corporations in Section 11 BewG. For listed shares, the lowest price on the valuation date applies; otherwise the value is derived from sales between unrelated third parties or from earnings prospects.

Sum of the fair market values of the individual assets less debts. Under Section 11(2) BewG it forms the lower limit for business valuation for tax purposes, but it is not a yardstick for the value of a going concern.

Court proceedings to review compensation payments (Abfindung and Ausgleich), for example under Sections 304, 305 AktG or Section 327b AktG. The court estimates the appropriate amount under Section 287 ZPO, usually on the basis of an expert opinion under IDW S1.
